items.explanation: London expected a quick win, but commanders like Howe and Burgoyne proved ordinary, while Loyalist support, colonial disunity, and the Royal Navy's limits all disappointed British planners.
options: A. They expected their generals to win easily
B. Loyalists were numerous throughout the colonies
C. The Continental Army lacked discipline
D. The Royal Navy was unmatched
items.stem: At the war's outset, British confidence rested on all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. British confidence rested on Loyalist numbers, colonial disunity, and the Royal Navy, not on brilliant generalship: commanders like Howe and Burgoyne proved ordinary, and Washington matched them in the field.
option_explanations.B: Loyalists were a real basis of British confidence: perhaps a fifth to a third of colonists remained loyal to the crown, a substantial internal base.
option_explanations.C: The Continental Army's lack of discipline was a real basis of British confidence: at the war's outset it was a raw, untrained force next to professional British regulars.
option_explanations.D: The Royal Navy's supremacy was a real basis of British confidence: it was unmatched in the world and could blockade, transport troops, and bombard coastal towns.

items.explanation: The 1783 treaty recognized independence and granted the trans-Appalachian west, but Canada remained British and Loyalists were promised a chance to recover confiscated property.
options: A. The west beyond the Appalachians went to the Americans
C. Quebec and its surroundings were ceded to the Americans
D. Loyalists could seek return of seized property
items.stem: All of the following were in the Treaty of Paris of 1783 EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: This was in the treaty: Britain ceded the trans-Appalachian west, with the Mississippi as the new nation's western boundary.
option_explanations.B: This was in the treaty: Britain formally recognized the independence of the United States.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. Quebec and Canada were not ceded; they remained British, and the new United States–Canadian boundary ran along the Great Lakes.
option_explanations.D: This was in the treaty: Article V provided that Loyalists could seek the return of confiscated property through the state courts.

items.explanation: The specter of Shays haunted Philadelphia: the Constitution gave Congress power to tax, raise armies, and call forth the militia 'to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions.' Washington wanted energy in government, not a bill of rights for rebellion, disarmament, or the Articles' unanimity rule.
options: A. A bill of rights guaranteeing the right of rebellion
B. The prohibition of any national standing army
C. A federal government strong enough to tax, raise armies, and suppress insurrections
D. The requirement of unanimous state consent for federal action
items.stem: The fear Washington expresses in the letter most directly shaped which feature of the new Constitution?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I feel myself exceedingly obliged to you for the full & friendly communications in your letters... Commotions of this sort, like snow-balls, gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way to divide and crumble them."
—George Washington to Henry Knox on Shays's Rebellion, 1786 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The Constitution contains no bill of rights guaranteeing rebellion, and Washington was alarmed by the rebellion, not sympathetic to a right of revolt. The Bill of Rights came later, in 1791.
option_explanations.B: Washington wanted the opposite of banning a standing army. The Constitution authorized Congress to raise and support armies — the very power the Articles had lacked.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The specter of Shays haunted Philadelphia: the Constitution gave the federal government power to tax, raise armies, and call forth the militia to 'suppress Insurrections' — a government with energy enough to enforce its laws.
option_explanations.D: Unanimous state consent was the Articles' rule — the very paralysis the framers were escaping. The Constitution replaced it with ratification by nine states and majority rule in Congress.
